https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkiy.text: Türkiye joins Black Sea oil, gas exploration in Bulgaria News Economy July 31 2026 14:35:15 Türkiye joins Black Sea oil, gas exploration in Bulgaria Türkiye ’s state-owned Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO) has acquired a 33 percent stake in the oil and natural gas exploration license for the Khan Tervel Block in Bulgaria’s Black Sea waters, the Turkish Energy and Natural Resources Ministry announced on July 31. TPAO had previously announced on Feb. 18 that it would join exploration activities in the Khan Tervel Block 1-26, located within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ), under a license operated by Shell. Under a decision approved by the Bulgarian Council of Ministers on July 31, Shell was authorized to transfer 33 percent of its rights and obligations under the exploration license to TPAO, formally making the Turkish company a new license holder in the project. Following the transaction, the ownership structure of the exploration license stands at 42 percent for Shell, 33 percent for TPAO and 25 percent for OMV. Speaking after the agreement was signed on Feb. 18, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said the exploration block covers slightly more than 3,800 square kilometers and is located in close proximity to Türkiye’s Sakarya gas field in the Black Sea. “This block lies in an area that can be considered relatively close to our Sakarya gas field. Together with Shell, we will conduct seismic surveys in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone and, hopefully next year, proceed with an exploratory drilling campaign under a license that will remain valid for approximately five years,” Bayraktar said. In a separate decision, the Bulgarian government approved a pre-feasibility study prepared by state-owned gas transmission operator Bulgartransgaz for a proposed NATO fuel pipeline connecting Greece and Türkiye to Romania through Bulgaria. NATO will contribute 10 million euros ($11.5 million) toward financing the study. The planned pipeline aims to enhance the alliance’s logistical capabilities along its southeastern flank by establishing a dedicated overland corridor for the transport of military fuel, including jet fuel and diesel, to NATO forces. Photograph: Mike Blake/Reuters US universities Hedge fund CEO gives $3bn to Carnegie Mellon University in historic donation Unprecedented university donation from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin will go toward building a new Miami campus Marina Dunbar Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.13 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Carnegie Mellon University will receive an unprecedented $3bn donation from the billionaire investor Ken Griffin, making it the largest single donation in the history of US education . Griffin, 57, is the founder and CEO of Citadel, described as the most profitable hedge fund in history. The money is going toward a new Miami campus as well as big investments at the university’s longtime home in Pittsburgh. Part of the funding will be used to develop Carnegie Mellon’s presence in Miami, Florida , where Griffin lives and where Citadel is now headquartered. The rest will support priorities in Pittsburgh, including recruiting prominent academics and making attendance more affordable for students. The Miami campus will support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and PhD students, nearly 300 faculty and more than 600 staff members, with construction slated to begin in 2027. $1bn will go toward Carnegie Mellon’s computer science school and other priorities, including financial aid, Griffin and the university president, Farnam Jahanian, said. The school will be renamed the Kenneth C Griffin School of Computer Science. “Throughout our history, CMU has anticipated moments of profound technological change and responded with new ways of thinking and solving problems,” Jahanian said in a statement. “Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others.” Founded by the industrialist Andrew Carnegie, Carnegie Mellon is particularly known for computer science, artificial intelligence, robotics and the performing arts. Its School of Computer Science is ranked as the top undergraduate computer science program in the US. The planned Miami campus will take a different approach from the traditional academic-major model. According to the university, education there will instead be structured around “societal challenges”. The campus will concentrate on “challenge areas spanning human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation”. The expansion also reflects Griffin’s continuing investment in Miami and south Florida. Citadel moved its headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022, and Griffin has since increased his commitments to the region to about $2.4bn, according to Reuters. Those contributions include support for a Miami charter school network, the University of Miami, Miami Dade College, public schools and math tutoring. Griffin, whose net worth Forbes estimated at about $58bn, will also become a member of Carnegie Mellon’s board of trustees. The board already includes hedge fund billionaire David Tepper, a Carnegie Mellon graduate and donor. The announcement comes one week after Nike co-founder Phil Knight donated $1bn to establish an engineering college at the University of Oregon. Universities are increasingly seeking wealthy donors to expand science and tech programs as artificial intelligence drives economic changes. These large donations have generated concerns about how much influence the wealthy class has over higher education. Griffin has publicly criticized the use of political power for personal enrichment, emerging as one of the most vocal critics of Donald Trump and his administration on Wall Street. Earlier this year, he condemned how the president’s family appear to have made financial gain from their proximity to the White House. Photograph: REX/Shutterstock Donald Trump Trump urges calls to Arkansas senator in push for permanent daylight saving time President appeared to share phone number of Tom Cotton for people to call to push him to support measure Associated Press and Guardian staff Sat 3 Oct 2026 16.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump on Saturday put pressure on the US senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, urging Americans to call what appeared to be the personal cellphone number of his fellow Republican and the chair of the Senate intelligence committee. The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including the president and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness. Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the US are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it – and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill’s enactment. “For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill,” Trump wrote on social media, noting that passing the proposal would give professional golfers more time on the greens. “So, everyone in Arkansas … tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all.” Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. The Associated Press called the number, but no one answered – and the voicemail box was full. The Guardian also called and was greeted with a message from the service carrier saying, “The wireless customer you are calling is not available. Please try again later.” Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own on Saturday afternoon, though he is not the only Republican who opposes it. “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent daylight saving time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” he wrote. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.” Cotton wrote that many Arkansans wouldn’t get sunrise until 8am or 8.30am during the dead of winter if daylight saving time was permanent. In that case, at the height of winter, those in Seattle wouldn’t see sunrise until 9am; and in Williston, North Dakota, the sun wouldn’t rise until nearly 9.45am, Cotton wrote. But Trump, who is spending the day at his northern Virginia golf club before traveling to Ohio later Saturday, promptly fired back. “If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so,” Trump said. The president added that he believed “that is really putting Arkansas FIRST”. This is not the first time Trump has released personal information about a US senator. While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the US senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as “unfit for office” after Trump denigrated the military service of the US senator John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham’s personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones. Graham later became a close ally of Trump before dying in July. McCain died in 2018. A 2025 poll from the AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of US adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to reset clocks twice a year, while 47% are opposed and 40% are neutral. Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942 during the second world war. The Senate passed a bill in 2022 to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.
